metadata.title: Is classroom diversity related to citizenship competences of ethnic minority and majority students?
metadata.venue: The Journal of Social Studies Research

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2016 Dutch data (grade 8) with a nested students-within-classrooms design. To reduce bias from non-participation at both student and school levels, the authors state that student-level and school-level weights were included in all multilevel models. The manuscript does not report the exact weight variable names from the ICCS database, but it explicitly follows the ICCS technical guidance (Schulz, Carstens, et al., 2018) by incorporating both student and school weights. The analytic sample was further restricted by excluding four mixed-track classrooms and removing students with missing values so that the different model sets used the same sample.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses the Netherlands’ ICCS 2016 data for secondary students in grade 8 (second year of Dutch secondary school). Per school, students in one randomly selected grade 8 classroom participated. From the Dutch sample of 2812 students in 123 schools, the authors excluded four mixed-track classrooms (total 109 students) based on power considerations. They then excluded 138 students with missing values to ensure that the different sets of analyses used the same sample. The final analytic sample is 2565 students in 119 schools (and classrooms).

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Citizenship knowledge (knowledge test; PV-based scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (multilevel regression coefficient for ethnic diversity in Model 3: B = 0.07, SE = 0.15; not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 citizenship knowledge the study leveraged classroom ethnic diversity and student/classroom background controls (ethnic status, SES, perceived openness of classroom climate, and educational track) to predict citizenship knowledge, finding that classroom ethnic diversity was not related to students’ citizenship knowledge and that the diversity-by-ethnic-status interaction was also non-significant. This indicates that, in the Dutch tracked secondary system, increasing classroom ethnic diversity alone may not improve civic knowledge acquisition, suggesting policy should focus on instructional mechanisms and learning opportunities rather than relying on compositional diversity effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Trust in civic institutions (attitude scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (Model 3): ethnic diversity B = −0.52, SE = 0.14, p < .01.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 trust in civic institutions the study leveraged classroom ethnic diversity and student/classroom controls (ethnic status, SES, perceived openness of classroom climate, and urbanization) to predict trust in civic institutions, finding that classroom ethnic diversity was negatively related to students’ institutional trust (B = −0.52, SE = 0.14, p < .01). This indicates that compositional diversity may coincide with lower institutional trust in this context, suggesting that citizenship education and school climate interventions may be needed to protect trust outcomes when classrooms are more ethnically diverse.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Attitudes towards gender equality (attitude scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (Model 3): ethnic diversity B = 0.51, SE = 0.16, p < .01.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 support for gender equality the study leveraged classroom ethnic diversity and student/classroom controls (gender, SES, perceived openness of classroom climate, and average classroom SES) to predict gender-equality support, finding that classroom ethnic diversity was positively related to support for gender equality (B = 0.51, SE = 0.16, p < .01). This indicates that, contrary to a simple “diversity reduces civic attitudes” expectation, classroom diversity may be associated with greater endorsement of democratic equality norms, implying that schools can potentially harness diverse classrooms to strengthen equality-related citizenship attitudes.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Attitudes towards ethnic equality (attitude scale)
main_findings.target_variable: Support for equal rights for all ethnic groups
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (Model 3): ethnic diversity B = 0.54, SE = 0.15, p < .01.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 support for equal rights for all ethnic groups the study leveraged classroom ethnic diversity and student/classroom controls (ethnic status, SES, perceived openness of classroom climate, and educational track) to predict ethnic-equality support, finding that classroom ethnic diversity was positively related to support for equal rights for all ethnic groups (B = 0.54, SE = 0.15, p < .01). This indicates that classroom diversity may foster political tolerance/equality values even when it is associated with lower institutional trust, suggesting that citizenship curricula emphasizing equal rights and structured intergroup contact could be particularly effective in diverse classrooms.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 Expected electoral participation (attitude scale)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (Model 3): ethnic diversity B = 0.12, SE = 0.12; not significant.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2016 Netherlands Grade 8 expected electoral participation the study leveraged classroom ethnic diversity and student/classroom controls (gender, SES, urbanization, and average classroom SES) to predict expected electoral participation, finding that classroom ethnic diversity was not related to voting intentions. This indicates that diversity-related effects may be domain-specific across citizenship competences, implying that policy efforts should not assume uniform impacts on political participation intentions and should instead target the specific civic domains where effects are observed.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes ICCS 2016 Dutch data for grade 8 students (second year of Dutch secondary school), using a nested students-within-classrooms design across 119 schools and 2565 students after excluding four mixed-track classrooms and students with missing values. Citizenship knowledge is PV-based: the authors compute five plausible values and report model estimates as the average across the five PV models, while the four attitude outcomes are Likert/scale measures standardized in ICCS 2009. The authors estimate weighted multilevel models with student-level and school-level weights to account for non-participation bias and clustering. Results show no association between classroom ethnic diversity and citizenship knowledge, but diversity is negatively related to trust in civic institutions and positively related to support for gender equality and equal rights for all ethnic groups; diversity is unrelated to expected electoral participation. The study is cross-sectional, so causality cannot be inferred, and the analysis is not an ML predictive pipeline (no ML algorithms or ML validation metrics are reported).
